newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan refugee children receive Japanese gifts.
newsitem.headline: Afghan refugee children receive Japanese gifts.

text.p: Japanese girl scouts gave gifts to hundreds of Afghan refugee children on Monday in Pakistan's North West Frontier Province, a U.N. statement said.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said six Japanese girl scouts and their supervisor distributed "peace packs" containing gifts to the children on behalf of more than 50,000 Japanese girl scouts.

Each peace pack is intended for one Afghan child and includes exercise books, ballpoint pens, pencils, crayons, an eraser, a ruler, a toothbrush and tube of toothpaste, a T-shirt, bar of soap, comb, some socks, a toy and a message from the collectors.
Yoshie Sakai, the girls' supervisor, said the exercise would benefit both Afghan refugee children and the Japanese girls who became aware of problems faced by the impoverished refugees.
"The Afghan children receive a lot of educational items and other gifts, which they need and probably could not otherwise afford," he said.

"And in Japan, a whole generation of girls has been sensitised to the problems faced by refugees, as well as to the terrible damage caused by 18 years of war in Afghanistan. It has made them value peace."

The UNHCR statement said it was the third year that Japanese girls had collected peace packs for Afghan children under a global initiative by the UNHCR and the World Wide Association for Girl Guides and Girl Scouts, which has nine million members.
So far, scouts and guides from 52 countries have collected peace packs for refugee children in 34 countries.

UNHCR officials said they hoped it would be possible to distribute some of the peace packs inside Afghanistan, one of the world's poorest nations. But this would depend on the Islamic Taleban who control more than two-thirds of the country.
More than three million Afghan refugees have fled to Pakistan during the Soviet occupation of their homeland in the 1980s. Around a million now remain in Pakistan.
